image_description:
**1. Chart type**  
- **Scatter plot** with labeled points and a highlighted rectangular region.
- The **y-axis is on a log scale**.

**2. Layout techniques**  
- **No faceting or small multiples**.
- **No stacking**.
- Uses **direct labels** for points and a **shaded/outlined annotation region** (“New coronavirus”).

**3. Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Average number of people infected by each sick person | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Fatality rate | Quantitative | Position on y-axis (log scale) |
| Disease / outbreak name (e.g., MERS, Ebola, SARS, Measles, etc.) | Categorical/Nominal | Point identity via direct text labels |
| New coronavirus estimate region | Quantitative range annotation | Shaded rectangular area spanning x- and y-ranges; red label |

**Visible labeled disease categories:** MERS, Bird flu, Ebola, Spanish flu, SARS, Smallpox, Swine flu, Seasonal flu, Common cold, Polio, Chickenpox, Measles, and New coronavirus (as a highlighted estimate region).

I noticed that the coronavirus doesn't seem nearly as frightening, especially when compared to the extreme fatality rate of the bird flu, and the number of people affected by the measles. I don’t really understand how a disease that doesn't seem very serious when looking at this graph can have such an effect on our world currently. I mean something we should be more worried about is apparently the return of smallpox.

I wonder why the coronavirus is a box instead of a point. Where will the point be located when it becomes a point?

We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graph:  "Coronavirus and the Potential for Destruction or Not?" by Jude of Pasadena, CA, “The Dangerous Range of Disease” by Gracie of Western Guilford High School in Greensboro, NC, “Coronavirus Chaos” by Lauren of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, NJ, “Can the Coronavirus Go Up Against These Other Big Dog Diseases?” by Chanse of Academy for Software Engineering, New York City, and “Frequent and Fatal Diseases“ by Kiersten of St. John the Apostle School, Clark, NJ,
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, Feb. 27 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.
The next graph will be released in two days -- Friday, Feb. 28, with moderation on Wednesday, March 4.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic --  voter opinion polls on hot topics.
You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.
The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Headline: Chinese Response to Coronavirus Excessive?
     In this graph, I notice that the new coronavirus has a higher possible infectivity and higher amount of people infected by each sick person than some other serious diseases. It is deadlier than polio and more infectious than the common cold. However, it is less deadly than ebola, and smallpox and less infectious than measles and smallpox. I also notice that there is no set number for fatality rate or infection rate. Instead there is a red highlighted zone where it is thought to be. This shows how little data there still is on this virus. The fact that the zone of uncertainty places the death rate at anywhere from .1% to almost 5% and the infection rate from a little over 1 to almost 3 proves that more research should be done. 
         Due to the uncertainty about this virus, China has imposed a lockdown in Wuhan and surrounding areas to avoid spreading the virus. However, seeing that it is possible that the fatality rate is as low as .1% and that it is less deadly and infectious than most serious diseases makes me wonder if it is worth quarantining entire regions and restricting travel for millions. While there should still be quarantine for those confirmed infected and treatments should be a priority, perhaps the response, which had some adverse effects, like trapping vacationing foreigners in China, was too great. Hopefully, the spread of the coronavirus will soon be slowed and travel to China will be reopened.
